claims.source: Accordingly, NOVA2 ablation causes defects in vascular lumen formation in vivo (Giampietro et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Giampietro et al., 2015.

claims.claim: L1-ΔTM provides the first example of an immunoglobulin-like cell adhesion molecule converted into a soluble angiogenic factor through alternative splicing removal of the exonic sequence that encodes the transmembrane domain.
claims.source: To our knowledge, L1-ΔTM provides the first example of an immunoglobulin-like cell adhesion molecule converted into a soluble angiogenic factor through AS removal of the exonic sequence that encodes the TM domain.
claims.evidence: The claim is a novel finding based on the authors' research.

claims.claim: Extracellular L1-ΔTM can promote angiogenesis via both autocrine and paracrine stimulation.
claims.source: We discovered that ECs acquire angiogenic properties not only upon ectopic expression of L1-ΔTM, but also when exposed to exogenously added L1-ΔTM (either as CM or as a recombinant protein). This supports the notion that extracellular L1-ΔTM can promote angiogenesis via both autocrine and paracrine stimulation.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from experiments showing angiogenic effects of both cell-expressed and exogenously added L1-ΔTM.

claims.claim: L1CAM frequently engages in homophilic L1CAM-L1CAM interactions between adjacent cells in neurons.
claims.source: In different cellular contexts, such as neurons, L1CAM frequently engages in homophilic L1CAM-L1CAM interactions between adjacent cells, which underlie its function in cell-cell adhesion (Maness and Schachner, 2007).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Maness and Schachner, 2007.

claims.claim: L1-ΔTM stimulates endothelial cells by heterophilic interactions with different surface molecules.
claims.source: However, our experiments were conducted in two EC lines, moEC and luEC, that express no or very little endogenous L1CAM. This implies that, regardless of autocrine or paracrine activity, L1-ΔTM stimulates ECs by heterophilic interactions with different surface molecules.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from experiments in EC lines with no or low endogenous L1CAM.

claims.claim: The extracellular portion of L1CAM interacts with a wide spectrum of membrane proteins, including different integrins, CD24, NCAM, F11R, and neuropilins.
claims.source: Accordingly, the extracellular portion of L1CAM has been reported to interact with a wide spectrum of membrane proteins, including different integrins, CD24, NCAM, F11R, neuropilins, etc. (Haspel and Grumet, 2003).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Haspel and Grumet, 2003.

claims.claim: L1CAM has been proposed to interact with the FGFR signaling machinery in different experimental settings.
claims.source: Following the pioneering studies of Doherty and Walsh in neuronal systems (Williams et al., 1994), L1CAM has been proposed to interact with the FGFR signaling machinery in different experimental settings (Mohanan et al., 2013; Son et al., 2011; Zecchini et al., 2008), possibly entailing a direct binding between the two molecules (Kulahin et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Williams et al., 1994; Mohanan et al., 2013; Son et al., 2011; Zecchini et al., 2008; and Kulahin et al., 2008.

claims.claim: There is a functional interplay between L1-ΔTM and FGFR1 in endothelial cells.
claims.source: Our data show for the first time a functional interplay between L1-ΔTM and FGFR1 in ECs, and implicate it in L1-ΔTM-induced angiogenesis.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on the authors' experimental data showing FGFR1 activation and inhibition effects.

claims.claim: In neural cell types, NOVA2 is required for the inclusion of the L1CAM exons 2 and 27.
claims.source: In neural cell types, NOVA2 is required for the inclusion of the L1CAM exons 2 and 27 (Mikulak et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Mikulak et al., 2012.

claims.claim: NOVA2 is not required for the inclusion of L1CAM exons 2 and 27 in endothelial cells.
claims.source: This is not the case in ECs, where even upon ectopic over-expression of NOVA2 exons 2 and 27 are not included in the L1CAM mRNA (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: L1-ΔTM is not detected in human or mouse brain despite high expression of NOVA2 in the nervous system.
claims.source: Moreover, despite the high expression of NOVA2 in the nervous system (Yano et al., 2010; Giampietro et al., 2015), we did not detect L1-ΔTM in human or mouse brain (Figure 1), which implies that NOVA2 is not involved in the AS of exon 25 in neural cells.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 1 and citations to Yano et al., 2010 and Giampietro et al., 2015.

claims.claim: NOVA2 is significantly up-regulated in ovarian carcinoma vasculature as compared to vessels in healthy ovary.
claims.source: NOVA2 is significantly up-regulated in OC vasculature as compared to vessels in healthy ovary.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data comparing OC and normal ovary.

claims.claim: NOVA2 expression is detected only in the vascular endothelium of ovarian carcinoma.
claims.source: Of note, NOVA2 expression is detected only in the vascular endothelium of OC and, in particular, in the nucleus of ECs.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data showing nuclear NOVA2 staining in ECs.

claims.claim: NOVA2 has a prognostic value in ovarian carcinoma.
claims.source: It is remarkable that, in spite of such a restricted expression pattern, NOVA2 has a prognostic value in OC, given its association with shorter patients' survival.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by survival analysis showing correlation between NOVA2 expression and patient outcome.

claims.claim: NOVA2 is the only splicing regulatory factor reported to be upregulated in cancer vasculature.
claims.source: To the best of our knowledge, NOVA2 is the only SRF reported to be upregulated in cancer vasculature, including OC (this study) and colorectal carcinoma (Gallo et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on the authors' knowledge and citation to Gallo et al., 2018.

claims.claim: NOVA2-mediated alternative splicing might play a relevant role in the phenotypic and functional aberrancies of tumor vessels.
claims.source: This implies that NOVA2-mediated AS might play a relevant, yet underappreciated, role in the phenotypic and functional aberrancies of the tumor vessels (Carmeliet and Jain, 2011).
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from NOVA2 upregulation in tumor vasculature and cited to Carmeliet and Jain, 2011.

claims.claim: L1-ΔTM could serve as a new circulating biomarker of cancer-associated vasculature.
claims.source: Based on its specific up-regulation in OC vessels (and likely in other cancer types as well), we speculate that L1-ΔTM could serve as a new circulating biomarker of cancer-associated vasculature.
claims.evidence: The claim is speculative based on the specific expression of L1-ΔTM in tumor vessels.

claims.claim: Circulating L1-ΔTM could be harnessed for diagnostic and prognostic purposes in ovarian carcinoma.
claims.source: Circulating L1-ΔTM could be harnessed for diagnostic and prognostic purposes, ranging from the detection of primary and recurrent OC to monitoring the therapeutic response, all objectives that would improve dramatically the clinical management of OC patients.
claims.evidence: The claim is speculative about potential clinical applications of L1-ΔTM as a biomarker.

claims.claim: Endothelial cells express the non-neural isoform of L1CAM mRNA, which lacks exons 2 and 27.
claims.source: As shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1, ECs express the non-neural isoform of L1CAM mRNA, which lacks exons 2 and 27 (Schäfer and Altevogt, 2010).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and citation to Schäfer and Altevogt, 2010.

claims.claim: moEC express no or very little endogenous L1CAM.
claims.source: To test this hypothesis, we selected an immortalized endothelial cell line of murine origin, moEC (Lampugnani et al., 2002; Taddei et al., 2008), because it expresses no or very little endogenous L1CAM (Figure 2B) and, therefore, is amenable to gain-of-function studies.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 2B and citations to Lampugnani et al., 2002 and Taddei et al., 2008.

claims.claim: The upper band in L1-FL immunoblot represents the mature, fully glycosylated cell-surface form.
claims.source: Immunoblotting of total extracts from L1-FL-expressing cells showed the expected doublet pattern (Figure 2B), with the upper band representing the mature, fully glycosylated cell-surface form, and the lower band corresponding to the precursor form (Moulding et al., 2000; Zisch et al., 1997).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 2B and citations to Moulding et al., 2000 and Zisch et al., 1997.

claims.claim: The lower band in L1-FL immunoblot corresponds to the precursor form.
claims.source: Immunoblotting of total extracts from L1-FL-expressing cells showed the expected doublet pattern (Figure 2B), with the upper band representing the mature, fully glycosylated cell-surface form, and the lower band corresponding to the precursor form (Moulding et al., 2000; Zisch et al., 1997).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 2B and citations to Moulding et al., 2000 and Zisch et al., 1997.

claims.claim: L1-ΔTM-expressing moEC show a single band that migrates slightly faster than the lower band of L1-FL.
claims.source: In contrast, L1-ΔTM-expressing moEC showed a single band that migrated slightly faster than the lower band of L1-FL (Figure 2B), consistent with the deletion of exon 25.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: moEC express only FGFR1 among the four FGFR family members.
claims.source: Among the four FGFR family members, moEC express only FGFR1 (data not shown) (Giampietro et al., 2012), as previously reported for other EC types (Giacomini et al., 2016; Javerzat et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by unpublished data and citations to Giampietro et al., 2012; Giacomini et al., 2016; and Javerzat et al., 2002.

results.result: Endothelial cells express a novel alternatively spliced isoform of L1CAM lacking exon 25, a 135-nucleotide cassette exon. This isoform is predominantly found in endothelial cells from both human and mouse samples, as demonstrated by bioinformatics analysis and RT-PCR.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C4 are well-supported by bioinformatics analysis (ExonMine program), RT-PCR data from multiple tissues and EC lines (Figure 1B, C), and sequence characterization. The convergence of computational prediction and experimental validation across species provides strong evidence for this EC-specific splicing event.

results.result: Skipping of L1CAM exon 25 generates L1-ΔTM, a soluble isoform lacking the transmembrane domain that is released into the extracellular space in its mature, fully glycosylated form. This release is specific to endothelial cells and represents secretion of the entire molecule rather than proteolytic cleavage.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C20 are strongly supported by multiple lines of evidence: sequence analysis showing deletion of the transmembrane domain (Figure 2A), immunofluorescence showing cytoplasmic localization (Figure 2C), immunoblotting of conditioned media (Figure 2D), glycosylation experiments in GnTI(-) cells (Figure 2—supplement 1), and comparative analysis with B16 cells that lack L1-ΔTM expression. The data convincingly demonstrate that exon 25 skipping produces a secreted isoform.

results.result: L1-ΔTM exhibits angiogenic properties, enhancing tube formation in vitro and neovascularization in vivo. This activity can be blocked by neutralizing antibodies and occurs through both autocrine and paracrine mechanisms, as demonstrated by conditioned medium experiments, recombinant protein treatment, and morpholino-induced expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C21-C30 are well-supported by multiple functional assays: tube formation assays with overexpressing cells (Figure 3A), antibody neutralization experiments (Figure 3B), conditioned medium transfer experiments (Figure 3C), dose-dependent effects of recombinant protein (Figure 3D), morpholino-induced endogenous expression (Figure 3F), and in vivo Matrigel plug assays (Figure 3G). The convergence of gain-of-function, loss-of-function, and in vivo data provides strong evidence for angiogenic activity.

results.result: L1-ΔTM-induced angiogenesis requires FGFR1 signaling. Treatment with recombinant L1-ΔTM increases FGFR1 phosphorylation, and FGFR1 inhibition abolishes L1-ΔTM-dependent tube formation.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C34 are supported by phosphorylation assays showing increased pFGFR1 upon L1-ΔTM treatment (Figure 3H) and functional rescue experiments with FGFR1 inhibitor PD173074 (Figure 3I). However, the mechanism of interaction (direct vs. indirect) remains unclear, and the sample size for phosphorylation quantification appears limited (n=3). Additional experiments such as co-immunoprecipitation or proximity ligation assays would strengthen the mechanistic claims.

results.result: NOVA2 directly regulates L1CAM exon 25 skipping in endothelial cells by binding to YCAY motifs within the exon. This regulation is specific to NOVA2 (not hnRNP A1 or SRSF3), conserved between mouse and human, and specific to exon 25 (not exons 2 or 27).
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C48 are strongly supported by multiple complementary approaches: bioinformatics prediction (SFmap), minigene splicing assays (Figure 4B), site-directed mutagenesis (Figure 4C), RNA-seq analysis, gain- and loss-of-function experiments in multiple EC lines (Figure 4E, F), CLIP assays demonstrating direct binding (Figure 4G), and conservation analysis. The convergence of computational, genetic, and biochemical evidence provides robust support for NOVA2-mediated regulation.

results.result: NOVA2 and L1-ΔTM are upregulated in ovarian carcinoma vasculature, where L1-ΔTM levels correlate with vessel density and NOVA2 expression correlates with poor patient survival. This suggests NOVA2-mediated L1-ΔTM production contributes to tumor angiogenesis.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C57 are supported by immunohistochemistry showing increased NOVA2 and L1CAM in OC vessels (Figure 5A, B), RT-PCR detection of L1-ΔTM in HOC-ECs (Figure 5C), correlation between L1-ΔTM and vessel density (Figure 5D, r=0.7671, p<0.01), and survival analysis from TCGA data (Figure 5E, HR=1.486, p=0.003). However, the sample size for correlation analysis is small (n=13), and causality is not established—these are associative findings that would benefit from functional validation in tumor models.

results.result: L1-ΔTM represents a novel class of angiogenic factor: an immunoglobulin-like cell adhesion molecule converted to a soluble form through alternative splicing of the transmembrane domain, acting via heterophilic interactions and both autocrine/paracrine mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Claims C58, C78, C79, and C81 represent summary conclusions well-supported by the collective experimental evidence. The novelty claim (C78) is reasonable given the literature search, though comprehensive verification of 'first example' claims is challenging. The heterophilic interaction inference (C81) is logical given experiments in cells lacking endogenous L1CAM, though direct identification of binding partners is lacking.

results.result: There is a functional interplay between L1-ΔTM and FGFR1 in endothelial cells.
results.evaluation: Claim C84 is supported by the phosphorylation and inhibitor data (C31-C34), demonstrating functional connection. However, the molecular mechanism (direct binding vs. indirect signaling) remains undefined. The claim is appropriately cautious in stating 'interplay' rather than 'direct interaction.'

results.result: NOVA2 regulation of L1CAM splicing is cell-type specific: NOVA2 does not regulate exons 2 and 27 in endothelial cells (unlike in neural cells) and does not regulate exon 25 in neural cells (despite high NOVA2 expression).
results.evaluation: Claims C86, C87, and C47 are supported by RT-PCR data in ECs overexpressing NOVA2 (Figure 1—supplement 1), absence of L1-ΔTM in brain tissue (Figure 1), and CLIP data showing no NOVA2 binding to exons 2/27 regions (Figure 4G). This demonstrates important cell-type specificity, though the molecular basis for this specificity is not elucidated.

results.result: L1-ΔTM could serve as a circulating biomarker for cancer-associated vasculature with diagnostic and prognostic applications in ovarian carcinoma.
results.evaluation: Claims C93 and C94 are explicitly speculative ('could serve,' 'could be harnessed') and lack experimental validation. No data on circulating L1-ΔTM levels, detection methods, or clinical utility are provided. While the tumor-specific expression provides rationale, these remain hypotheses requiring future validation studies.

results.result: Background information on L1CAM structure, processing, expression patterns, alternative splicing in general, and NOVA2 function is provided through citations to prior literature.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C85 represent background knowledge supported by appropriate citations to established literature. These provide necessary context but are not novel findings of this study.

results.result: NOVA2 is significantly upregulated specifically in ovarian carcinoma vascular endothelium (nuclear localization) and has prognostic value. NOVA2 is the only splicing regulatory factor reported to be upregulated in cancer vasculature, suggesting NOVA2-mediated alternative splicing plays an important role in tumor vessel abnormalities.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C92 are supported by immunohistochemistry data (Figure 5A, Figure 5—supplement 1) and survival analysis (Figure 5E). The 'only SRF' claim (C91) is appropriately qualified ('to the best of our knowledge') and cites supporting evidence. Claim C92 is appropriately presented as inference ('might play') rather than established fact.

results.result: Methodological details regarding L1CAM isoform expression in endothelial cells, including characterization of the non-neural isoform, selection of moEC cell line for gain-of-function studies, and immunoblot interpretation of L1-FL glycosylation states.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C100 represent methodological details and characterization supported by experimental data (Figure 1—supplement 1, Figure 2B) and appropriate citations. These provide important technical context for interpreting the main findings.
